q: Which teeth have a single pointed cusp and are used mainly for gripping and tearing food?
x: Canines are the pointed teeth beside the incisors, used to grip and tear food. Incisors cut, while premolars and molars crush and grind.

q: The dental formula of an adult human shows that each half of the upper jaw contains:
x: Each half jaw of an adult has 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars, which is 8 teeth. Eight teeth in each of the four half jaws gives the full set of 32.

q: The 'wisdom teeth', usually the last teeth to appear, in the late teens or later, are the:
x: Wisdom teeth are the third (last) molars at the back of each half jaw. They erupt last, usually from the late teens onwards, and sometimes not at all.

q: A child's 20 milk teeth are later replaced by 32 permanent teeth. Which permanent teeth grow without any milk tooth before them?
x: The milk set has 8 incisors, 4 canines and 8 molars. Permanent incisors and canines replace their milk forms and the premolars replace the milk molars, so the 12 permanent molars have no milk predecessors.

q: The root of a tooth is covered by a thin, bone-like layer that helps fix the tooth in its socket. This layer is the:
x: Cementum covers the root and, with the fibres of the periodontal ligament, holds the tooth in the jaw socket. Enamel covers only the crown, and dentine lies beneath both.

q: The part of a tooth that lies hidden inside the socket of the jaw bone is the:
x: The root is embedded in the jaw socket. The crown is the exposed part above the gum, and the neck is the narrow region at the gum line.

q: The salivary glands that lie in the floor of the mouth directly under the tongue are the:
x: 'Sublingual' means under the tongue. The parotids lie in front of the ears and the submandibular glands lie along the inner side of the lower jaw; tonsils are lymphoid tissue, not salivary glands.

q: Which of the following is NOT a role of the tongue in the mouth?
o: Rolling chewed food into a bolus
Pushing the bolus back into the pharynx
x: The muscular tongue mixes food with saliva, shapes it into a bolus, pushes it back for swallowing and carries taste buds. Salivary amylase is made by the salivary glands, not the tongue.

q: During swallowing, food is prevented from entering the nasal cavity because the:
o: Soft palate and uvula rise to close off the nasal passage
Hard palate moves down onto the tongue
x: The soft palate with its uvula is raised to seal the passage to the nose. The epiglottis protects the windpipe, not the nasal cavity, and the hard palate is fixed bone that cannot move.

q: The roof of the mouth, which separates the oral cavity from the nasal cavity, is formed by the:
o: Soft palate in front and hard palate behind
Hard palate alone, made entirely of bone
Hard palate in front and soft palate behind
x: The palate forms the roof of the mouth: the bony hard palate in front and the muscular soft palate, ending in the uvula, behind. It lets a person chew and breathe at the same time.

q: In the neck and chest, the oesophagus lies:
o: In front of the trachea, just under the skin
Behind the trachea and in front of the vertebral column
Inside the cartilage rings of the trachea
Beside the trachea but outside the thoracic cavity
x: The oesophagus runs down behind (dorsal to) the trachea and in front of the backbone, through the thorax, and then pierces the diaphragm. The tracheal rings are open at the back, where the oesophagus lies.

q: Which statement about the oesophagus is correct?
o: It secretes amylase to continue starch digestion
Its glands secrete mucus but no digestive enzymes
It absorbs water and simple sugars
Its wall has no muscle, so food falls by gravity
x: The oesophagus only carries food to the stomach. Its glands make mucus for lubrication; it secretes no enzymes, absorbs nothing, and moves food by peristalsis, not gravity.

q: The stomach lies in the:
o: Lower right part of the abdomen, near the appendix
Upper left part of the abdomen, just below the diaphragm
Pelvic cavity, above the urinary bladder
x: The J-shaped stomach lies in the upper left abdomen, immediately below the diaphragm, with the liver mostly to its right.

q: Food entering the stomach from the oesophagus passes through which regions of the stomach, in order, before reaching the duodenum?
x: Food enters at the cardiac end (near the heart), is churned in the large body, with the fundus bulging above, and leaves through the pyloric region and pyloric sphincter into the duodenum.

q: Gastric glands in the stomach wall pour their secretions into the stomach through tiny openings in its lining called:
x: The stomach mucosa is dotted with gastric pits, into which the gastric glands open. Rugae are the large folds of the empty stomach, and villi and crypts belong to the small intestine.

q: The longest part of the human alimentary canal is the:
x: The small intestine is several metres long, far longer than the large intestine (about 1.5 m), which gives time and surface for digestion and absorption.

q: Intestinal juice is produced mainly by tubular glands that open between the bases of the villi. These glands are the:
x: The crypts of Lieberkühn are pits between the villi whose cells secrete intestinal juice. Gastric glands are in the stomach, the islets are endocrine tissue in the pancreas, and the parotids are salivary glands.

q: The mucus that protects and lubricates the lining of the intestine is secreted by scattered cells in its epithelium called:
x: Goblet cells are mucus-secreting cells scattered among the columnar cells of the intestinal lining. Parietal and chief cells are in gastric glands, and Kupffer cells are in the liver.

q: At the junction of the ileum with the large intestine there is a valve. Its main role is to:
o: Release bile into the large intestine
Stop air from entering the colon
Control the passing of faeces from the rectum
Stop the contents of the caecum flowing back into the ileum
x: The ileocaecal valve lets material pass from the ileum into the caecum but prevents backflow. Faeces are controlled by the anal sphincters, and bile enters at the duodenum.

q: Which statement correctly compares the large intestine with the small intestine?
o: It is wider but shorter, and its lining has no villi
It is longer and narrower, with more villi
It is wider and longer, with larger villi
It is narrower but shorter, and secretes more enzymes
x: The large intestine is only about 1.5 m long but wider in diameter. Its lining has no villi and secretes mucus rather than digestive enzymes.

q: Which statement about the human vermiform appendix is correct?
o: It has no known digestive role, but it can become inflamed (appendicitis)
It secretes enzymes that digest cellulose
It is the main site of water absorption
x: In humans the appendix plays no part in digestion and is regarded as a vestigial organ. If it becomes blocked and infected, it is inflamed: appendicitis.

q: Which statement about the position of the liver is correct?
o: It lies in the lower left abdomen
It lies in the thorax, between the lungs
It lies in the pelvic cavity, behind the bladder
It lies in the upper right abdomen, just below the diaphragm
x: The liver, the largest gland, occupies the upper right part of the abdomen just under the diaphragm, partly covering the stomach.

q: The cystic duct connects the:
o: Gall bladder to the common bile duct
x: The cystic duct leads from the gall bladder and joins the hepatic duct from the liver to form the common bile duct, which opens into the duodenum.

q: Bile is made by the liver all the time but is released into the gut mainly after meals. Between meals, bile travels by which route?
o: Liver → common bile duct → duodenum → gall bladder
Liver → hepatic duct → cystic duct → gall bladder
x: Between meals the sphincter at the duodenal end of the common bile duct is closed, so bile from the hepatic duct backs up the cystic duct into the gall bladder for storage. After a meal it flows out through the common bile duct to the duodenum.

q: Saliva contains an enzyme that helps protect the mouth by attacking the cell walls of bacteria. This enzyme is:
x: Lysozyme in saliva (and tears) breaks down bacterial cell walls. Lipase digests fats, pepsin digests proteins in the stomach, and maltase digests maltose.

q: In infants, an enzyme in gastric juice curdles milk so that it stays longer in the stomach for protein digestion. This enzyme is:
x: Rennin converts soluble milk protein (caseinogen) into insoluble curd (casein), so pepsin has time to act. Renin, spelt with one n, is a kidney enzyme that helps control blood pressure.

q: Inactive pepsinogen secreted into the stomach is converted into active pepsin by:
x: Hydrochloric acid from the parietal cells activates pepsinogen to pepsin, and pepsin then activates more. Enterokinase activates trypsinogen in the duodenum, and gastrin is a hormone, not an activator.

q: Although little absorption takes place in the stomach, which substance can be absorbed to some extent through the stomach wall?
x: The stomach can absorb some alcohol and certain drugs such as aspirin. Amino acids and fatty acids are absorbed in the small intestine, and starch must be digested before any absorption.

q: Pepsin works best in a medium that is:
x: Pepsin works in the stomach, where hydrochloric acid keeps the pH at about 2. Pancreatic enzymes, by contrast, work in the slightly alkaline duodenum.

q: Starch that escapes digestion in the mouth is digested mainly in the small intestine by:
x: Pancreatic juice contains amylase, which continues breaking starch into maltose in the duodenum. Pepsin and rennin act on proteins, and lipase on fats.

q: Trypsin from the pancreas breaks proteins into smaller peptides. It works in the:
o: Acidic conditions of the large intestine
Alkaline conditions of the small intestine
x: Trypsin acts in the duodenum, where bicarbonate from pancreatic juice and bile makes the contents alkaline. This is the opposite of pepsin, which needs the acid of the stomach.

q: Lactase in the small intestine digests milk sugar (lactose) into:
x: Lactose is a disaccharide of glucose and galactose, so lactase releases these two. Sucrase gives glucose and fructose, and maltase gives two glucose molecules.

q: After drinking milk, an adult regularly gets bloating and diarrhoea, but has no problem eating bread or table sugar. The most likely cause is:
o: Too little lactase in the small intestine
Too little sucrase in the small intestine
Too much hydrochloric acid in the stomach
x: Milk sugar is lactose. Without enough lactase it stays undigested in the gut, where bacteria ferment it and cause gas and diarrhoea. Normal tolerance of bread (starch) and table sugar (sucrose) shows that amylase and sucrase are working.

q: The final digestion of peptides into amino acids in the small intestine is carried out by:
x: Peptidases, together called erepsin, in the intestinal juice and on the epithelial cells finish protein digestion to amino acids. Pepsin only makes polypeptides, bile has no enzymes, and lipase acts on fats.

q: Which statement about bile is correct?
o: It contains lipase that digests fats
It is acidic and helps pepsin to work
It is made and stored by the pancreas
It contains bile salts but no digestive enzymes
x: Bile contains no enzymes; its bile salts emulsify fats, and its alkalinity helps neutralise acid chyme. It is made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

q: A gallstone blocks a person's common bile duct. Which of the following is expected?
o: Undigested starch in the faeces and low blood glucose
Failure of protein digestion in the stomach
Darker faeces and increased absorption of fats
Pale, fatty faeces and poor absorption of vitamin K
x: Without bile, fats are poorly emulsified and absorbed, so they appear in the faeces, which are also pale because bile pigments are missing. Fat-soluble vitamins such as K are absorbed with fats, so their uptake falls.

q: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, excess glucose reaching the liver is stored there as:
x: The liver converts excess glucose into glycogen, the animal storage polysaccharide, and breaks it down again when blood glucose falls. Starch and cellulose are plant polysaccharides.

q: Excess amino acids cannot be stored. In the liver their amino groups are removed and turned into urea. Removal of the amino group is called:
x: Deamination removes the amino group, which becomes ammonia and is then converted into urea; the rest of the molecule can be used for energy. Emulsification is the action of bile on fats.

q: Jaundice, a yellow colour of the skin and the whites of the eyes, develops when:
o: Too much bile is released into the duodenum
The pancreas fails to secrete lipase
Bilirubin builds up in the blood, as when bile flow is blocked or the liver is diseased
Too much glycogen is stored in the liver
x: Bilirubin, a yellow bile pigment from broken-down haemoglobin, is normally removed by the liver in bile. If the liver is damaged or bile cannot drain, it accumulates in the blood and tissues.

q: Which statement about swallowing is correct?
o: It is entirely voluntary from the mouth to the stomach
It starts voluntarily, then continues as an automatic reflex once food reaches the pharynx
It is entirely a reflex and cannot be started at will
It depends on gravity, so it cannot happen when lying down
x: The tongue pushes the bolus back voluntarily; once it touches the pharynx, the swallowing reflex and then peristalsis take over. Because peristalsis moves the food, swallowing works even upside down.

q: Dental caries (tooth decay) begins when:
o: Fluoride in water softens the dentine
The pulp cavity fills with cementum
Bacteria in plaque ferment sugars into acids that dissolve the enamel
x: Plaque bacteria feed on sugars left on the teeth and produce acids, which dissolve the enamel and then the dentine. Fluoride actually makes enamel more resistant to acid.

q: Glucose continues to be absorbed from the ileum even when its concentration in the lumen is lower than in the epithelial cells. This shows that glucose is absorbed by:
x: Moving glucose against its concentration gradient needs carrier proteins and energy, which is active transport. Simple and facilitated diffusion only move substances down a gradient, and osmosis is the movement of water.

q: Humans cannot digest the cellulose in plant food because they:
o: Have a stomach too weak to grind it
Absorb cellulose whole without digesting it
Do not produce the enzyme cellulase
x: No human digestive gland secretes cellulase, so cellulose passes through undigested as dietary fibre (roughage). This fibre adds bulk to the faeces and helps peristalsis.

q: Gastric juice begins to flow when a hungry person merely sees or smells food. This early secretion is caused by:
o: Nerve impulses from the brain to the stomach (a reflex)
x: The sight, smell, taste or thought of food sends nerve impulses from the brain to the gastric glands before any food arrives. Stretching and gastrin act later, once food is in the stomach, and secretin acts on the pancreas.

q: Besides making the gall bladder contract, the hormone cholecystokinin (CCK) also stimulates the:
o: Stomach to secrete more hydrochloric acid
Pancreas to secrete a juice rich in enzymes
x: CCK is released by the duodenum when fats and proteins arrive. It empties the gall bladder and makes the pancreas release enzyme-rich juice, while secretin mainly causes a watery bicarbonate juice.

q: Which sequence shows the enzymes that act on a protein, in order, as it is digested from food into amino acids?
x: Protein digestion starts with pepsin in the stomach, continues with pancreatic trypsin in the duodenum, and ends with peptidases of the small intestine, which release amino acids.

q: Heartburn, a burning pain behind the breastbone, occurs when:
o: Bile flows back into the liver
Pepsin digests the wall of the colon
Acidic stomach contents pass back into the oesophagus through a weak cardiac sphincter
Food enters the trachea instead of the oesophagus
x: The cardiac sphincter normally stops stomach contents rising. If it is weak, acid refluxes into the oesophagus, whose lining lacks the stomach's thick mucus protection, causing a burning feeling. It has nothing to do with the heart.
